newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda tribunal imposes tight media restrictions.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda tribunal imposes tight media restrictions.

text.p: Journalists covering the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda on Wednesday got their first taste of the heavy security and tight media restrictions at forthcoming trials.
Tribunal staff gave the media their rules at the tribunal headquarters in the international conference centre in Arusha, northern Tanzania.
"To walk around this building you have to have an escort and you have to understand that security is very, very, very tight," tribunal spokeswoman Beatrice Lacoste told reporters.

The court met in camera to hear a defence request that a Rwandan Hutu charged with genocide and crimes against humanity be released on medical grounds. The first trial is supposed to start on Thursday but could be adjourned.
Around 40 journalists from Africa, Europe and the United States gathered in Arusha, an attractive holiday destination but handicapped by appalling telecommunications.
"There will be no TV today. There will be no impromptu pictures and no impromptu interviews," Lacoste told Reuters.
The journalists were confined to a large press room lacking telephones, tables and with only two power sockets.
"It's basically still all being arranged," Lacoste said.

Tribunal officials remain sensitive to comparisons with a parallel tribunal on war crimes in the former Yugoslavia held in the Hague, arguing the Hague tribunal benefits from its location in a first world city and a larger budget.
"The Hague is perfectly equipped. It has cameras, monitors, everything, so it is very easy to send faxes and make phone calls," Lacoste said.
Some officials say the Rwanda tribunal is a poor relation and underfunded. But deputy prosecutor Honore Rakotomanana told Reuters last week the Rwanda tribunal's 1996 budget was about $36 million.
The tribunal was created by the United Nations after the genocide in Rwanda between April and June 1994, when up to one million Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus were exterminated.
Its mandate is to try the top organisers and main perpetrators of the genocide rather than the tens of thousands of rank and file killers.

The tribunal, which last sat in May but is yet to begin formal trials, has so far indicted only 21 people and has only three of them in its custody. The guilty face a maximimum penalty of life imprisonment.
